questions.title: Configuring a Consumer Group to Read a Topic in Parallel
questions.prompt: A Kafka topic orders has 6 partitions. Write the consumer configuration (group.id and the relevant settings) for 3 consumer instances that should split the topic's partitions between them for parallel processing, and explain what happens if you start a 7th consumer instance in that same group.
questions.modelAnswer: group.id is what defines membership in a consumer group -- all 3 consumer processes set the identical group.id value (e.g., 'orders-processor'), and Kafka's group coordinator assigns a disjoint subset of the topic's partitions to each active member, so with 6 partitions and 3 consumers, each gets 2 partitions and no two consumers in the group ever read the same partition at the same time, giving parallel, non-overlapping processing. If a 7th consumer joins that same group.id, a rebalance is triggered, but there's nothing left to give it: since there are only 6 partitions and the other consumers already hold at least one each, the 7th instance sits idle with zero partitions assigned until some other consumer in the group leaves -- more consumers than partitions is not an error, it's just wasted capacity, since a partition is the unit of parallelism and can only be read by one consumer in a group at a time.
questions.professionalAnswer: The key setting is just making sure all 3 consumer instances run with the exact same group.id -- that's literally what tells Kafka they're one logical group splitting the work, not three independent readers. With 6 partitions and 3 consumers sharing a group.id, Kafka's coordinator hands out 2 partitions to each one, and I never have to write that assignment logic myself. The interesting part is the 7th-consumer question, because it's a common point of confusion: people expect an error, but what actually happens is nothing dramatic -- a rebalance runs, tries to find an unassigned partition for the new consumer, and there isn't one, so it just sits there connected but idle. That's worth knowing specifically because it means scaling a consumer group past its partition count doesn't get you more throughput; the partition count is the real ceiling, not the number of consumer processes you're willing to run.
questions.example:
consumer_config = {
    "bootstrap.servers": "broker1:9092,broker2:9092",
    "group.id": "orders-processor",
    "auto.offset.reset": "earliest",
}
# Run this identical config in 3 separate consumer processes/instances.
# Kafka's group coordinator assigns 2 of the 6 partitions to each one.
commonMistakes: Giving each consumer instance a different group.id, which makes them each read ALL partitions independently instead of splitting the work
Assuming more consumers always means more parallelism, missing that partition count is the real ceiling
Expecting the 7th consumer to cause an error instead of just sitting idle
Not understanding that a rebalance (partition reassignment) happens whenever group membership changes
keyPoints: Consumers sharing the same group.id split a topic's partitions between them
A partition can only be actively read by one consumer within a group at a time
Partition count is the hard ceiling on a consumer group's parallelism
Extra consumers beyond the partition count sit idle, not erroring, until a rebalance frees a partition

Correctly explains partition-to-consumer assignment for 6 partitions / 3 consumers
Correctly explains the idle-7th-consumer outcome
Config/code is valid and relevant

questions.title: Diagnosing a deadlock between two ETL jobs
questions.prompt: Two nightly stored procedures occasionally fail with a deadlock error when they run at overlapping times, each updating the same two tables. Explain what a deadlock is, how SQL Server resolves it automatically, and two concrete things you'd change to prevent it from recurring.
questions.modelAnswer: Blocking happens whenever one transaction needs a lock another transaction already holds, and simply waits -- this is normal and expected. A deadlock is the special case where Transaction A is waiting on a lock held by Transaction B, while B is simultaneously waiting on a lock held by A -- neither can ever proceed. SQL Server detects this automatically and picks one transaction as the 'deadlock victim,' rolling it back and raising an error, while the other transaction proceeds normally. To prevent recurrence: (1) access the two tables in the same order in both procedures -- a common deadlock cause is two transactions locking the same two tables in opposite order; and (2) keep transactions as short as possible, doing only what genuinely needs to be atomic inside BEGIN/COMMIT, so locks are held for the shortest possible window and the overlap that triggers the deadlock has a smaller chance of occurring.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start by reassuring whoever's asking that blocking itself isn't a bug -- it's how isolation is enforced any time two transactions genuinely need the same data at the same moment. A deadlock is the specific, more serious case: A is waiting on a lock B holds, B is waiting on a lock A holds, and neither can ever win -- it's a true standoff. SQL Server doesn't just hang forever; it detects the cycle and picks a 'deadlock victim' to roll back automatically, which is why the application sees an error and needs to retry. For the actual fix, the first thing I'd check is whether both procedures touch the two tables in a different order -- that's the single most common cause, and standardizing the access order so both procedures always touch, say, Table A before Table B usually eliminates it outright. Second, I'd look at whether either transaction is doing more than it needs to inside BEGIN/COMMIT -- unrelated reads, validation logic -- and trim the transaction down to just the atomic part, since shorter transactions hold locks for less time and collide less often.
commonMistakes: Treating a deadlock the same as ordinary blocking -- blocking is normal, a deadlock is a genuine, unresolvable standoff
Assuming SQL Server will just hang forever instead of recognizing it auto-detects and resolves deadlocks
Fixing the symptom by adding a retry loop in the application without addressing the inconsistent table access order
Making a transaction longer by adding error handling or logging inside it, which increases lock duration
keyPoints: Blocking is normal; a deadlock is two transactions waiting on each other with no way out
SQL Server auto-detects deadlocks and rolls back a chosen 'victim' transaction
The victim's application should retry the transaction
Accessing tables in a consistent order across procedures prevents most deadlocks
Shortening transactions reduces how long locks are held and how often collisions occur

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes blocking from a deadlock
Correctly explains SQL Server's automatic deadlock resolution

Proposes shortening transactions as a concrete fix

questions.title: A query got slow after it used to be fast
questions.prompt: A report query that filters WHERE YEAR(OrderDate) = 2013 used to run instantly and now takes minutes as the table has grown. There is an index on OrderDate. Diagnose why the index isn't helping, and rewrite the WHERE clause so it is.
questions.modelAnswer: The predicate is non-SARGable: wrapping the OrderDate column in the YEAR() function forces SQL Server to compute YEAR(OrderDate) for every single row before it can compare against 2013, which means the index on the raw OrderDate column can't be used -- it stores actual dates, not year-extracted values. This was barely noticeable on a small table (a full scan of a few hundred rows is instant either way), but as the table grows into the millions of rows, the same non-SARGable predicate turns a sub-second query into one that takes minutes. The fix is to rewrite the condition so the column itself is left untouched, and transform the comparison value instead: WHERE OrderDate >= '2013-01-01' AND OrderDate < '2014-01-01'. This asks the identical logical question but lets SQL Server use the index on OrderDate to jump directly to the matching range.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is a textbook SARGability problem, and the giveaway is right there in the WHERE clause -- there's a function wrapped around the column. Any time I see YEAR(SomeDateColumn), UPPER(SomeColumn), or similar, my first instinct is: the index on that raw column can't be used, because SQL Server would have to transform every row's value before it could compare it, and an index doesn't store transformed values. The reason it 'used to be fast' is simply table size -- a full scan is invisible on a small table and brutal on a large one, so this kind of bug often doesn't show up until data volume grows past some threshold. The fix is always the same shape: stop transforming the column, and transform the comparison value instead. Instead of asking 'what year is this date in,' I ask 'is this date within the 2013 calendar year range' -- same answer, but now the raw OrderDate column is untouched in the comparison, so the existing index can be used for a range scan instead of a full scan.
commonMistakes: Blaming the index itself ('the index must be corrupt/fragmented') instead of the predicate wrapping the column
Rewriting to BETWEEN '2013-01-01' AND '2013-12-31' and accidentally excluding rows with a time component on Dec 31
Not recognizing other common non-SARGable patterns like UPPER(column) = 'X' or a leading-wildcard LIKE '%text'
Assuming the problem only appears with YEAR() and missing that any function on the column causes the same issue
keyPoints: SARGable means the predicate can use an index directly; non-SARGable forces a full scan
Wrapping the column in a function (YEAR, UPPER, etc.) makes a predicate non-SARGable
Fix by transforming the comparison value instead of the column
The performance gap only becomes visible as table size grows

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the predicate as non-SARGable and explains why
Correctly explains why this matters more as the table grows

questions.title: A report is hanging, but there's no deadlock error
questions.prompt: Users report that a dashboard query has been 'just spinning' for several minutes, but no deadlock error ever appears. Explain the difference between this situation and a deadlock, how you'd identify the actual head blocker, and what you'd check before deciding to kill the blocking session.
questions.modelAnswer: This is ordinary blocking, not a deadlock -- a deadlock is a genuine standoff that SQL Server detects and resolves automatically within seconds by killing a victim; it never just hangs indefinitely. Plain blocking, by contrast, can hang as long as whatever is holding the lock keeps holding it, because there's no cycle for SQL Server to detect -- one session is simply waiting its turn behind another, and nothing resolves that automatically. To find the actual head blocker, I'd query sys.dm_exec_requests, specifically looking at the blocking_session_id column -- the session with a non-zero blocking_session_id is being blocked, and the session that ID points to (which itself usually shows blocking_session_id = 0) is the head blocker actually holding the lock everyone's waiting on. Before killing that session, I'd check what it's actually doing -- its SQL text, and whether it's an open, uncommitted transaction (an application that opened a transaction and is sitting idle, or a long-running batch job that's legitimately mid-write). Killing a session mid-write rolls back whatever it was doing, which can be worse than the wait itself if it's a large, mostly-finished operation -- so I'd rather understand what it's doing and consider letting it finish or committing/rolling it back cleanly than reflexively kill it.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd clarify, because it changes the whole response, is that this isn't a deadlock -- SQL Server resolves deadlocks on its own, usually within seconds, by picking a victim and rolling it back. If nothing has errored and the query is just sitting there, that's plain blocking: one session waiting on a lock another session is holding, with no cycle, so nothing forces a resolution automatically. My first query is always against sys.dm_exec_requests, looking at blocking_session_id -- that tells me directly who's blocked and, by following the chain, who the actual head blocker is, as opposed to the session that looks blocked but is itself only blocked by someone else further up. Once I've got the head blocker's session ID, I'd pull its actual SQL text and check whether it's sitting inside an open transaction that was never committed, versus genuinely mid-execution on a big write. That distinction decides what I do next -- if it's an application bug that opened a transaction and forgot to close it, killing the session is reasonable and I'd also flag that bug separately. If it's a legitimate long-running batch load that's 90% done, killing it rolls back all of that work and probably makes things worse, so I'd rather let it finish, or coordinate with whoever owns that job before touching it.
questions.example:
-- Find who's blocking whom
SELECT session_id, blocking_session_id, wait_type, wait_time, status
FROM sys.dm_exec_requests
WHERE blocking_session_id <> 0;

-- Follow the chain to the head blocker (blocking_session_id = 0, but others point to it)
-- Then inspect what the head blocker is actually running:
SELECT text
FROM sys.dm_exec_requests r
CROSS APPLY sys.dm_exec_sql_text(r.sql_handle) t
WHERE r.session_id = @HeadBlockerSessionId;
commonMistakes: Treating any hanging query as a deadlock, when a true deadlock is auto-resolved within seconds, not left hanging
Killing the first blocked session found instead of tracing blocking_session_id to the actual head blocker
Killing a session without checking whether it's mid-write on a legitimate long-running job
Not distinguishing an application bug (an abandoned open transaction) from a genuinely busy, legitimate session
keyPoints: A hanging query with no error is ordinary blocking, not a deadlock -- deadlocks auto-resolve quickly
sys.dm_exec_requests' blocking_session_id column traces the blocking chain to the actual head blocker
Check what the head blocker is actually doing before killing it -- an abandoned transaction vs. a legitimate long write
Killing a session mid-write rolls back its work, which can be worse than waiting for it to finish

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes ordinary blocking from a deadlock
Correctly identifies how to find the head blocker (sys.dm_exec_requests / blocking_session_id)
Explains what to check before killing the blocking session
Provides correct, relevant diagnostic SQL

questions.title: A Covering Index Isn't Helping, and Nobody Knows Why
questions.prompt: A table has a nonclustered index covering exactly the columns a report query needs, but the query's execution plan still shows a full scan instead of using the index. The query is SELECT * FROM Sales.SalesOrderDetail WHERE ProductID = 712. What's the most likely cause, and how would you fix the query?
questions.modelAnswer: SELECT * is almost certainly the cause. A covering index only helps when the query asks for columns the index actually includes; SELECT * asks for every column in the table, regardless of what's actually needed, which defeats the index's coverage the moment even one requested column isn't part of it. SQL Server then has to fall back to either a Key Lookup for each matching row or a full scan, depending on cost, instead of satisfying the query entirely from the narrower index. The fix is to name only the columns the report genuinely needs instead of SELECT *: SELECT SalesOrderID, ProductID, OrderQty, UnitPrice FROM Sales.SalesOrderDetail WHERE ProductID = 712. If those four columns are exactly what the covering index includes, the optimizer can now satisfy the entire query from the index alone, without ever touching the underlying table.
questions.professionalAnswer: Before touching the index, I'd actually look at the execution plan and the exact columns requested, because 'should use the index but doesn't' almost always traces back to the SELECT list, not the index definition. SELECT * is the first thing I'd check, because it's such a common habit and such a direct cause: if the index only covers four specific columns and the query asks for all fifteen columns on the table via *, the index simply can't satisfy that request on its own, and SQL Server has to go fetch the rest from the table itself — either via a Key Lookup per row or by abandoning the index entirely for a full scan, depending on how many rows are involved. The fix is almost always just naming the specific columns the report actually displays instead of *. I'd also double check that the index's included columns genuinely match what the report needs, because if even one required column is missing from the index, the same fallback happens no matter how narrowly I write the SELECT list.
commonMistakes: Assuming the index itself must be broken or missing, without checking what columns the query actually requests
Rebuilding or recreating the index before checking the SELECT list, missing the actual cause
Not verifying the index's included columns genuinely cover everything the trimmed SELECT list needs
Fixing this one query but not checking other queries against the same table for the identical SELECT * habit
keyPoints: SELECT * requests every column, defeating a covering index that only includes some of them
The fallback is a Key Lookup per row, or a full scan, instead of satisfying the query from the index alone
The fix is naming exactly the columns actually needed
The index's included columns must still genuinely match what's requested for this fix to work

Correctly explains why it defeats a covering index
Provides a correct fix naming specific columns

questions.title: The Pipeline Shows "Succeeded" Even Though a Copy Activity Failed
questions.prompt: An Azure Data Factory pipeline has a Copy activity whose Upon Failure path connects to a cleanup activity. Last night the Copy activity genuinely failed, the cleanup ran successfully, and the pipeline's overall run status still shows "Succeeded." Is this a bug? Explain what's actually happening and how you'd change the design if you want a failed Copy to make the whole pipeline show red.
questions.modelAnswer: This isn't a bug — it's the Try-Catch pattern behaving exactly as designed. Data Factory determines overall pipeline status only by looking at leaf activities, the ones with nothing connected downstream of them. Here, only Upon Failure is defined from the Copy activity, routing to the cleanup activity; there's no Upon Success or Upon Skip path defined from the Copy activity itself feeding into anything else, so the cleanup activity (which succeeded) is the only leaf activity Data Factory evaluates, and a successful leaf means the pipeline reports Succeeded — the Copy activity's own failure is absorbed rather than surfaced. To make a failed Copy actually show red at the pipeline level, switch to a Do-If-Else pattern: define both an Upon Failure path (to the cleanup/error handler) and an Upon Success path from the Copy activity, each leading to further downstream activities — with both paths now feeding leaf activities, a failure on the Copy activity side becomes a failure on a leaf activity, and the overall pipeline status reports Failure.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell them it's genuinely not a bug, even though I understand why it looks like one at first glance — this is Try-Catch doing exactly what it's designed to do. The key detail is that Data Factory only looks at leaf activities — the ones with nothing after them — to decide whether the whole pipeline succeeded or failed. In this design, the only thing defined after the Copy activity is its Upon Failure path into the cleanup activity, so when the cleanup activity finishes successfully, that's the only leaf activity in the picture, and a successful leaf means a successful pipeline, full stop — the Copy activity's own failure never gets to 'vote' on the overall status because nothing is watching for it at the top level. If they want a failed Copy activity to actually make the pipeline go red — say, so a downstream alert fires — the fix is to switch to Do-If-Else: define both an Upon Failure and an Upon Success path out of the Copy activity, each leading somewhere, so now both outcomes are being tracked as leaf-level paths instead of only the failure path being absorbed by the handler.
commonMistakes: Assuming this is a bug in Data Factory rather than the designed behavior of leaf-activity status evaluation
Confusing the Try-Catch pattern (absorbs failure, reports success) with Do-If-Else (surfaces failure)
Not recognizing that only leaf activities (nothing downstream) determine overall pipeline status
Trying to fix this by adding more logging inside the cleanup activity instead of restructuring the activity paths
keyPoints: Pipeline status is determined only by leaf activities -- ones with nothing downstream
Try-Catch (only Upon Failure defined) absorbs the failure and reports overall success
Do-If-Else (both Upon Failure and Upon Success defined) surfaces the failure to the pipeline level
This is intended behavior, not a bug

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains this is intended Try-Catch behavior, not a bug
Correctly explains the leaf-activity status evaluation rule
Proposes the correct Do-If-Else fix
Explains why Do-If-Else changes the outcome

questions.title: A Task Has Been Stuck in 'up_for_retry' for an Hour
questions.prompt: A task in a DAG you own has been sitting in up_for_retry state for over an hour, well past its retry_delay, and hasn't actually retried. The DAG run itself still shows as running. What would you check, in what order, to figure out why it isn't actually retrying?
questions.modelAnswer: First, check whether this is really a retry-timing issue or a scheduler problem — up_for_retry just means the task is waiting for the scheduler to re-queue it once retry_delay has passed, so the scheduler is the one actually responsible for acting on that; a stalled, crashed, or overloaded scheduler won't pick up any task waiting to retry, no matter how far past its delay it is. Second, check pool or worker-slot capacity — if the task's pool (or the executor's available worker slots) is fully occupied by other running tasks, a task that's eligible to retry still can't actually start until a slot frees up, which looks identical to 'stuck' but is really 'queued behind capacity.' Third, check DAG- and task-level concurrency settings like max_active_runs and task concurrency limits, since an overly restrictive limit can silently prevent an otherwise-ready task from starting even when the scheduler and workers are both healthy.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first instinct wouldn't be to look at the task's own retry settings — up_for_retry is a normal, boring state, and the question is really 'why hasn't the scheduler acted on it yet.' So first I'd check scheduler health itself: is it actually running, is it backed up, are other DAGs also showing delayed task pickup right now, which would point at a systemic scheduler problem rather than anything specific to this one task. Second, I'd check whether this task sits in a pool, and whether that pool (or the executor's worker slots generally) is fully saturated by other tasks — a task that's perfectly ready to retry still waits its turn if there's no slot open for it, and that's an extremely common cause that has nothing to do with the retry_delay setting at all. Third, I'd look at the DAG's own concurrency settings, because a restrictive max_active_runs or task-level concurrency limit can quietly block a task from starting even when everything upstream of it looks healthy. Only after ruling those three out would I start doubting the task's own retry configuration.
commonMistakes: Assuming the retry_delay setting itself is misconfigured before checking whether the scheduler or worker pool is actually healthy
Not checking pool/worker slot capacity, which can make a perfectly healthy task look permanently stuck
Restarting the whole DAG run instead of diagnosing the actual bottleneck first
Overlooking DAG-level concurrency settings (max_active_runs, task concurrency) that can silently block a ready task
keyPoints: up_for_retry means waiting for the scheduler to re-queue the task after retry_delay, not an error by itself
Check scheduler health first, since a stalled scheduler acts on no task at all
Check pool/worker slot capacity, which can block a ready task from actually starting
Check DAG/task-level concurrency settings that can silently prevent execution

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what up_for_retry actually means
Checks scheduler health as a first, logical step
Checks pool/worker capacity as a likely cause
Checks DAG/task concurrency settings

questions.title: A Nightly Write Fails With a Schema Mismatch Error
questions.prompt: A nightly job that appends new rows to a Delta table silver_orders starts failing overnight with a schema mismatch error, after the upstream source added a new discount_code column. Explain why Delta Lake rejects this write by default, and the two different ways you could legitimately fix it depending on whether you actually want that new column kept.
questions.modelAnswer: Delta Lake enforces schema on write by default -- schema enforcement -- meaning any append whose DataFrame schema doesn't exactly match the target table's existing schema is rejected outright rather than silently reshaping either the data or the table; this is deliberate, protecting a table from silently absorbing bad or unexpected structure. Here the upstream source added a genuinely new column, discount_code, that the existing table has never seen, so the incoming DataFrame's schema no longer matches. Fix 1 (new column should be kept going forward): enable schema evolution for this specific write using the mergeSchema option (or ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMNS for an explicit, deliberate change), which adds discount_code to the table's schema and backfills it as null for all existing historical rows -- appropriate when the new column is a genuine, wanted addition to the table going forward. Fix 2 (new column should NOT be kept, at least not yet): explicitly drop the discount_code column from the incoming DataFrame before the write, keeping the existing schema exactly as it was -- appropriate if the column is premature, not yet reviewed, or not meant for this table at all. The wrong move in either case is turning off schema enforcement broadly or blindly enabling schema evolution everywhere, since that would also let a genuine upstream mistake (a renamed or malformed column) slip through unnoticed.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain that this failure is actually Delta doing its job, not malfunctioning -- schema enforcement exists specifically to reject a write that doesn't match the table it's writing to, rather than silently reshaping either side. Here the real cause is upstream: a new discount_code column showed up that the table's current schema has never seen. From there it's genuinely a judgment call, not a single fix. If this column is something the team actually wants captured going forward, I'd enable schema evolution for this one write -- the mergeSchema option, or an explicit ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMNS -- which adds the column and backfills every existing row with null for it. If it's not something we want yet, maybe it's premature or hasn't been reviewed, I'd just drop it from the incoming DataFrame before writing, leaving the table's schema untouched. What I wouldn't do is turn on mergeSchema globally as a blanket setting, because that quietly removes the protection schema enforcement was giving us in the first place -- I want this to be a deliberate decision each time, not a default.
questions.example:
-- Fix 1: deliberately evolve the schema to add the new column
df.write.format("delta").mode("append").option("mergeSchema", "true").saveAsTable("silver_orders")

-- Fix 2: deliberately exclude the new column instead, keeping the existing schema
df.drop("discount_code").write.format("delta").mode("append").saveAsTable("silver_orders")
commonMistakes: Globally disabling schema enforcement instead of handling this one deliberate change
Using mergeSchema=true reflexively without first checking whether the new column is actually wanted
Confusing mergeSchema (adds new columns) with overwriteSchema (replaces the entire schema, used with overwrite mode)
Not considering that mergeSchema backfills existing rows with null for the new column, which may or may not be the right default
keyPoints: Schema enforcement rejects a write whose schema doesn't exactly match the target table by default, deliberately
mergeSchema=true (or ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMNS) is the fix when the new column should genuinely be added
Explicitly dropping the new column before the write is the fix when it shouldn't be kept yet
The decision should be deliberate per-write, not a blanket toggle

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why schema enforcement rejects the write
Correctly describes the mergeSchema/add-column fix and when it's appropriate
Correctly describes the drop-the-column fix and when it's appropriate
Warns against a blanket/reflexive fix

questions.title: Yesterday's Numbers Changed After the Fact
questions.prompt: A gold-layer daily sales summary for Tuesday showed $42,000, but when the same report is rerun on Thursday, Tuesday's number has quietly changed to $45,800, with no code deployment in between. Walk through the most likely explanation and what you'd check to confirm it.
questions.modelAnswer: The most likely explanation is late-arriving data: some source records for Tuesday's sales didn't actually land in the bronze layer until after Tuesday's pipeline run had already processed and aggregated the day, and when the pipeline re-ran on a later day and reprocessed or re-aggregated Tuesday's partition, those late rows were now present and included, changing the total. This is common with upstream systems that batch-export with their own delay, or with retries/corrections applied after the fact. To confirm: check the bronze layer for Tuesday's partition at two points in time -- the row count/content as of when Tuesday's original gold number was computed versus the row count now -- if the bronze count for Tuesday's partition genuinely grew between those two checks, that confirms late-arriving data rather than, say, a bug in the aggregation logic itself (which would typically affect many days' numbers, not just reshape one specific day inexplicably). Also check whether the pipeline's silver/gold logic actually reprocesses historical partitions on each run (which exposes it to late data) versus only ever appending the current day (which wouldn't have changed Tuesday at all) -- understanding which processing model is in place is itself diagnostic information about whether this is even possible.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first instinct is late-arriving data, not a code bug, specifically because nothing was deployed between the two runs -- if the logic itself hadn't changed, the most plausible explanation for a number changing is that the underlying data changed. I'd go check Tuesday's partition in the bronze layer and compare its row count now against what it would have had to be at the time the original $42,000 number was computed, which I can often reconstruct from pipeline run logs or a bronze-layer audit column. If that count genuinely grew, that confirms it -- some rows for Tuesday simply hadn't arrived yet when the first pass ran. I'd also check whether this pipeline's design even reprocesses historical partitions on each run or only ever appends the newest day, because that tells me whether late data reaching Tuesday's partition after the fact was even possible given how the pipeline is built, versus pointing me toward a different explanation entirely if it's append-only.
commonMistakes: Assuming a code bug changed the number without first checking whether the underlying source data itself changed
Not distinguishing a pipeline that reprocesses historical partitions from one that only appends new data, which changes what's even possible here
Treating a 'the number changed and we don't know why' report as acceptable instead of tracing the root cause before reporting a new number as correct
Not considering that late data could keep arriving, meaning even the new Thursday number for Tuesday might not be final
keyPoints: Late-arriving source data reprocessed into a historical partition is the most common explanation for a day's number changing after the fact
Confirm by comparing bronze-layer row counts/content for that date across two points in time
Whether the pipeline reprocesses historical partitions versus only appends matters to the diagnosis
A number that already changed once may not be fully final, which is worth flagging

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies late-arriving data as the likely cause
Describes a concrete way to confirm it (comparing bronze layer over time)
Distinguishes a reprocessing pipeline design from an append-only one
Notes that the number may still not be final

questions.title: Consumer Lag Is Climbing and Nobody Changed Anything
questions.prompt: A Kafka consumer group's lag (the gap between the latest produced offset and the group's committed offset) has been steadily climbing for two hours on a topic whose production rate hasn't changed. No consumer has crashed. What would you check, and what's the most likely explanation if you also notice frequent rebalance events in the consumer group's logs?
questions.modelAnswer: Climbing lag with a stable production rate and no crash points to consumers not keeping up with processing, not an ingestion problem -- the fix-worthy question is why consumption slowed, not why production sped up. First check: per-partition lag (not just the group total) to see whether it's evenly spread or concentrated on specific partitions, which would point at a hot/skewed key rather than a general capacity problem. Second check: consumer-side processing time per message/batch -- a downstream dependency (a database write, an API call) that got slower would show up here directly. If the logs also show frequent rebalances, that's very likely both a symptom and a cause feeding each other: a rebalance pauses all consumption in the group while partition assignment is recalculated, so frequent rebalances alone can account for real lag growth independent of any per-message slowness. Frequent rebalancing is commonly caused by a consumer's processing time per poll exceeding max.poll.interval.ms, which makes the broker think that consumer died and kick it out, triggering a rebalance -- which then causes the next consumer to also run slow or time out, triggering another rebalance, in a self-reinforcing cycle. The fix is usually tuning max.poll.interval.ms upward, max.poll.records downward (so each poll's batch is smaller and faster to process), or addressing whatever downstream slowness is making processing exceed the poll interval in the first place.
questions.professionalAnswer: Since production hasn't changed and nothing crashed, I'd immediately focus on the consumption side rather than assuming anything about ingestion. I'd pull per-partition lag first, not just the group total, because an even spread points at a general capacity problem while lag piling up on one or two specific partitions points at a hot key instead. I'd also check how long processing is actually taking per poll on the consumer side, since a downstream dependency getting slower -- a database write, an external API call -- shows up exactly as climbing lag with no crash. The detail about frequent rebalances is the real tell, though: a rebalance pauses the entire group's consumption while partitions get reassigned, so frequent rebalances alone can explain a lot of this lag on their own. And frequent rebalancing almost always traces back to a consumer's processing time exceeding max.poll.interval.ms -- the broker assumes that consumer died, kicks it out, triggers a rebalance, and if the next consumer is also running slow, the cycle just repeats. I'd tune max.poll.interval.ms up or max.poll.records down, or dig into why processing got slow enough to trip that threshold in the first place.
commonMistakes: Checking only the group's total lag instead of per-partition lag, missing a skewed/hot partition
Assuming a crash caused the lag when the question states no consumer crashed
Not connecting frequent rebalances to max.poll.interval.ms being exceeded by slow processing
Fixing this by just adding more consumer instances without checking whether partition count/assignment is actually the bottleneck
keyPoints: Stable production with climbing lag points to a consumption-side slowdown, not an ingestion problem
Check per-partition lag to rule out a skewed/hot partition
A rebalance pauses all consumption in the group while reassigning partitions
Frequent rebalances are commonly caused by processing time exceeding max.poll.interval.ms, creating a self-reinforcing cycle

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses a consumption-side (not production-side) slowdown
Proposes checking per-partition lag and processing time
Correctly explains the rebalance-pauses-consumption mechanism
Correctly connects frequent rebalances to max.poll.interval.ms

questions.title: terraform apply Is Stuck Saying the State Is Locked
questions.prompt: A teammate's terraform apply crashed partway through (their laptop lost power) and now every terraform plan or apply anyone on the team runs fails immediately with a state lock error. Explain what the lock is actually protecting against, why it's now stuck, and the right way to resolve it versus the risky shortcut people sometimes take.
questions.modelAnswer: Terraform's state lock exists to prevent two people (or two CI runs) from modifying the same state file concurrently, which could otherwise corrupt the state or produce a result where Terraform's recorded idea of infrastructure no longer matches reality -- it's a safety mechanism, not a bug getting in the way. Normally the lock is acquired at the start of a plan/apply and released automatically when it finishes; the problem here is that the laptop lost power mid-apply, so the process that held the lock never got to release it cleanly, leaving the lock held indefinitely with no actual operation still running. The right way to resolve it is terraform force-unlock <lock-id>, using the specific lock ID shown in the error message -- but critically, only after confirming no apply is actually still running somewhere (checking with the teammate, checking CI, checking the backend directly if it's something like an Azure Storage blob lease) -- force-unlocking while an apply genuinely is still in progress elsewhere is the risky shortcut, because it can let two applies run concurrently against the same state after all, defeating the entire purpose of the lock and risking real corruption. Separately, it's worth checking whether the crashed apply left any resources partially created that the state doesn't yet reflect, since a mid-apply crash can also cause state drift independent of the lock issue.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain the lock isn't an obstacle, it's doing exactly what it's supposed to do -- preventing two plan/apply operations from touching the same state file at the same moment, which could otherwise corrupt it or leave it out of sync with real infrastructure. The reason it's stuck is simple: the process that held the lock never got to release it, because the laptop lost power before the apply finished. The right fix is terraform force-unlock with the specific lock ID from the error message, but I'd never run that without first confirming nothing else is genuinely still applying -- checking with the teammate directly, checking whether any CI job is mid-run, maybe checking the backend's lock state directly if that's possible. Force-unlocking while something actually is still running defeats the whole point of having a lock and risks two applies racing against the same state, which is a much worse problem than being temporarily blocked. I'd also take a look at whether the crashed apply left anything half-created in real infrastructure that the state file doesn't know about yet, since that's a separate drift issue the lock alone won't reveal.
commonMistakes: Running terraform force-unlock reflexively without first confirming no apply is genuinely still running elsewhere
Deleting the state file's lock entry manually in the backend instead of using force-unlock with the correct lock ID
Not checking for resources partially created by the crashed apply that might now be drifted from state
Treating the lock as a bug to work around rather than a safety mechanism doing its job
keyPoints: The state lock prevents concurrent modifications that could corrupt state or desync it from real infrastructure
A crashed process can leave the lock held indefinitely with nothing actually running
terraform force-unlock with the specific lock ID is the correct fix, but only after confirming nothing is genuinely still running
A crashed mid-apply can also leave real state drift worth checking for separately from the lock itself

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the purpose of the state lock
Correctly explains why it's stuck after the crash
Correctly describes force-unlock as the fix, with the safety check first
Mentions checking for state drift from the crashed apply

questions.title: Data Stopped Showing Up in the KQL Database
questions.prompt: A Fabric Eventstream has been feeding a KQL database's table for weeks, and this morning the table simply stopped receiving new rows -- no error banner is showing anywhere obvious. Walk through where you'd check, in order, to find out where the data is actually getting stuck.
questions.modelAnswer: Work backward through the pipeline rather than guessing. First, check the Eventstream's own monitoring view to confirm it's actually still receiving events from its source (an Event Hub, IoT Hub, or similar) -- if the upstream source itself stopped sending (a producer-side outage, an expired connection string, a stopped device) the Eventstream has nothing to forward regardless of anything downstream, and that's genuinely the most common real cause. Second, if events are confirmed arriving at the Eventstream, check the Eventstream's transformation/processing nodes and its destination configuration specifically -- a transformation that started throwing errors on a new, unexpected event shape (e.g., a new field or a malformed value) can silently drop or fail to route events without a loud top-level error. Third, check the destination side directly -- the KQL database's data connection (or update policy) that's supposed to receive the Eventstream's output; a credential expiring, a renamed table, or a permissions change on the KQL database can break ingestion from the Eventstream side with the failure surfacing (if at all) in the destination's own ingestion diagnostics rather than the Eventstream's view. Checking source-to-destination, in that order, isolates which specific hop actually broke instead of guessing at the whole pipeline.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd work through this hop by hop rather than assuming the problem is wherever I happen to look first. Step one is the Eventstream's own monitoring view -- is it actually still receiving events from its source at all? That's genuinely the most common cause: an upstream producer went quiet, a connection string expired, a device stopped sending, and the Eventstream has nothing to even forward. If events are clearly arriving there, step two is looking at the transformation nodes inside the Eventstream and its destination routing -- a transformation that started choking on a new or malformed event shape can silently drop events without throwing anything loud at the top level. Step three, if the first two look clean, is the destination side specifically -- the KQL database's ingestion connection, checking for an expired credential, a renamed table, or a permissions change, since that kind of failure often shows up (if it shows up at all) in the destination's own diagnostics rather than anywhere visible from the Eventstream side. Going through it in that order tells me exactly which hop broke instead of restarting the whole thing and hoping.
commonMistakes: Assuming the KQL database itself is broken before checking whether the Eventstream is even still receiving upstream events
Not checking the Eventstream's own monitoring view, which usually shows throughput dropping to zero at a specific, identifiable time
Overlooking that a destination-side credential or permission change can break ingestion without an obvious Eventstream-side error
Restarting the whole Eventstream reflexively instead of isolating which specific hop actually failed
keyPoints: Work backward (or forward) through the pipeline's hops rather than guessing at the whole thing
Check the Eventstream's monitoring view first to confirm whether upstream events are even arriving
A transformation node can silently drop/fail on an unexpected new event shape
A destination-side (KQL database connection/credential) issue can break ingestion with no obvious Eventstream error

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Proposes a logical, ordered diagnostic approach across the pipeline's hops
Correctly identifies checking the Eventstream's upstream source/monitoring first
Correctly identifies transformation nodes as a possible silent failure point
Correctly identifies the destination/KQL connection as a possible failure point

questions.title: Choosing a clustering key for a new fact-staging table
questions.prompt: You're designing a new staging table that will be loaded nightly and queried immediately afterward by ProductID ranges. A table can have only one clustered index. Explain the difference between a clustered and nonclustered index, and what makes a good choice of clustering key.
questions.modelAnswer: A clustered index determines the actual physical order rows are stored in on disk -- which is exactly why a table can have only one: data can only be physically sorted one way. A nonclustered index is a separate structure that holds a sorted copy of the indexed column(s) plus a pointer back to the actual row, and a table can have many of them. Looking up a row through the clustering key is fastest, since SQL Server navigates directly to the physical location; looking up through a nonclustered index takes one extra step -- find the index entry, then follow the pointer back to the row. A good clustering key is narrow (a small data type, since every nonclustered index secretly stores the clustering key as its row pointer), unique (no ambiguity about physical order), and ever-increasing (so new rows append at the end instead of forcing existing rows to physically shuffle). Given the staging table is loaded nightly and then range-queried by ProductID, an ever-increasing identity key for the clustered index, with a nonclustered index on ProductID to support the range queries, is the more defensible design than clustering directly on ProductID.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd frame this as two separate decisions. First: what should the table's physical row order be -- that's the clustered index, and I only get one shot at it. Second: what other lookup patterns do I need to support cheaply -- that's where nonclustered indexes come in, and I can have several. For a staging table that's loaded nightly, I actually lean toward an ever-increasing identity column as the clustering key rather than ProductID directly, even though ProductID is the column people will query by. The reason is load performance: an ever-increasing key means new rows always append at the end of the physical order, so the nightly load doesn't cause page splits from inserting into the middle of existing data. Then I add a nonclustered index on ProductID to support the range queries -- yes, that costs one extra pointer-following step per lookup compared to clustering directly on ProductID, but it's a much smaller cost than the load-time page-splitting I'd get from clustering on a column that isn't naturally ordered or unique.
commonMistakes: Assuming more indexes are always better without considering the nightly load's insert cost
Choosing a wide, non-unique column as the clustering key, which bloats every nonclustered index that secretly carries it as a pointer
Forgetting a table can have only one clustered index, and trying to 'cluster' on two different columns
Not connecting the ever-increasing key recommendation to the specific nightly-load write pattern described in the scenario
keyPoints: Clustered index = physical row order, one per table
Nonclustered index = separate structure with a pointer back to the row, many allowed
Good clustering key: narrow, unique, ever-increasing
Design choice should weigh load (insert) pattern against query (read) pattern

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the clustered vs. nonclustered distinction
Correctly lists the three traits of a good clustering key
Applies the tradeoff to the specific nightly-load scenario given
Recommends a nonclustered index to support the ProductID range queries

questions.title: Designing an Incremental Nightly Load for a Growing Table List
questions.prompt: A data team currently has five Azure Data Factory pipelines, one hardcoded per source table, copying each table nightly. The table list changes every few months as new sources are added. Propose a better pipeline design, and explain the tradeoff it introduces.
questions.modelAnswer: Five hardcoded, nearly-identical pipelines is a maintenance burden that grows every time a table is added or removed, since each change means building and testing a whole new pipeline rather than updating a configuration value. The better design is a single parameterized pipeline driven by a Lookup activity that reads the current table list from a configuration source — a control table, or a config file — with firstRowOnly set to false so it returns every row as an array, feeding a ForEach activity whose Items reference that array. Inside the ForEach, a single Copy activity, parameterized by @item() for the table name, handles the actual copy for whatever table that iteration is on. Adding or removing a source table becomes a one-row change to the configuration table, with zero changes to the pipeline itself. The tradeoff is that debugging becomes slightly less direct: a failure now surfaces inside a generic loop iteration rather than a pipeline with that table's name baked into it, and sequential-vs-parallel execution has to be decided carefully across all five-plus tables at once rather than independently per pipeline, since they now share one loop's settings.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd consolidate all five into one pipeline, driven by configuration rather than hardcoding each table into its own copy of nearly identical pipeline logic. The pattern is a Lookup activity at the start, reading the current table list from a small control table with firstRowOnly set to false so I get the whole list back as an array, feeding directly into a ForEach activity. Inside that ForEach, one Copy activity does the actual work, parameterized by @item() for whichever table that iteration is currently on. The real win is that adding the team's sixth or seventh source table six months from now becomes a single new row in a configuration table, with nobody touching the pipeline itself at all. I'd be upfront about the tradeoff, though: when something breaks at 2 AM, the error now says 'the ForEach iteration for table X failed' instead of 'the CustomerTable pipeline failed,' which is a half-step less direct to triage, and I'd also have to make one deliberate sequential-vs-parallel decision that now applies to every table in the list together, rather than being able to tune each pipeline's concurrency independently like before.
commonMistakes: Keeping five separate pipelines and just accepting the growing maintenance burden
Forgetting to set firstRowOnly to false on the Lookup, which would return only one row instead of the full table list
Not acknowledging the debugging tradeoff this consolidation introduces
Defaulting to parallel execution for all tables without checking whether any share a destination or resource
keyPoints: A Lookup activity with firstRowOnly: false feeds a ForEach the full table list
A single parameterized Copy activity inside the loop replaces five hardcoded pipelines
Adding a new source becomes a configuration change, not a pipeline change
The tradeoff is less direct debugging and a shared concurrency decision across all tables

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Proposes the Lookup + ForEach + parameterized Copy pattern
Correctly explains how this reduces future maintenance
Honestly identifies a real tradeoff this design introduces
Mentions firstRowOnly: false as a necessary Lookup setting

questions.title: Designing the Medallion Layers for a New IoT Sensor Feed
questions.prompt: A manufacturing client wants to onboard a new IoT sensor feed (temperature readings every 10 seconds from 500 machines) into their existing medallion lakehouse. Propose what bronze, silver, and gold should each look like for this specific feed, and call out one design decision that's genuinely different from a typical daily batch source.
questions.modelAnswer: Bronze should capture the raw sensor events essentially as received -- machine_id, timestamp, temperature_reading, and whatever metadata the feed includes, partitioned by ingestion date, appended via a streaming write (Autoloader or Structured Streaming) rather than a batch job, since the feed is continuous, not a daily drop. Silver should deduplicate (sensor feeds commonly resend due to retries), validate/flag out-of-range readings rather than silently dropping them (a sensor reporting -200°C is itself a signal, likely a hardware fault worth tracking, not just bad data to discard), and conform timestamps to a consistent timezone/format. Gold should aggregate to a business-relevant grain -- likely per-machine, per-hour (or per-shift) average/min/max temperature -- rather than exposing raw 10-second readings to dashboards, since nobody queries individual readings directly and the aggregation also dramatically reduces the row count a BI tool has to handle. The genuinely different design decision from a typical daily batch source: this pipeline should be built with Structured Streaming (bronze-to-silver, possibly silver-to-gold) rather than a scheduled batch job, because the whole value of 500 machines reporting every 10 seconds is lost if the pipeline only processes once a day -- but that also means handling late-arriving/out-of-order events and watermarking decisions that a daily batch job never has to think about at all.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd design bronze to take the feed almost exactly as it arrives -- machine ID, timestamp, reading, whatever metadata comes with it -- ingested continuously via Autoloader or Structured Streaming rather than a nightly job, because batching a 10-second feed once a day throws away the entire reason it reports that often. Silver is where I'd dedupe, since sensor retries sending the same reading twice is common, and I'd flag rather than discard anything wildly out of range, because a reading of -200°C is probably a broken sensor, which is itself useful information, not noise to filter out. Gold I'd aggregate to something a dashboard can actually use -- per-machine hourly min/max/average, not 500 machines' worth of raw 10-second points. The thing I'd flag as genuinely different here versus a normal batch source is that this whole pipeline needs to think about late and out-of-order events and watermarking, which a once-a-day batch job simply never has to deal with -- that's a real design cost that comes with the territory of actually getting streaming's value.
commonMistakes: Treating this like any other batch source and scheduling it nightly, losing the real-time value of a 10-second feed
Silently dropping out-of-range sensor readings in silver instead of flagging them as a potential hardware-fault signal
Exposing raw 10-second-grain readings directly to gold/dashboards instead of aggregating to a usable grain
Not considering deduplication in silver, when sensor/IoT feeds commonly resend due to network retries
keyPoints: Bronze should ingest the raw feed via streaming, not batch, given the continuous nature of the source
Silver should deduplicate and flag (not silently discard) out-of-range readings
Gold should aggregate to a usable grain (per-machine, per-hour) rather than exposing raw readings
Streaming ingestion introduces late/out-of-order event handling that a daily batch source wouldn't need

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Proposes a sensible bronze design appropriate to a streaming source
Proposes a sensible silver design including dedup and handling out-of-range values
Proposes a sensible gold aggregation grain
Correctly identifies the streaming-vs-batch design difference and its implications
