questions.title: Architecting a Real-Time Alerting Pipeline in Fabric
questions.prompt: A logistics company wants an alert sent the moment any delivery truck's GPS feed reports a stop lasting more than 15 minutes outside of a scheduled delivery window. Propose the Fabric components you'd chain together to build this, in order, and explain why a KQL database is the right fit for the "stop lasting more than 15 minutes" logic specifically.
questions.modelAnswer: Chain: the GPS feed streams into a Fabric Eventstream, which ingests and optionally lightly transforms the raw location events; the Eventstream routes into an Eventhouse/KQL database, which stores the time-series location events and is where the actual 'stop detection' logic runs as a continuous or scheduled KQL query (grouping by truck, looking at consecutive points with near-identical location/zero speed for a sustained duration); that KQL query's output (or a materialized view of it) feeds Activator, which watches for the specific condition (stop duration greater than 15 minutes, outside a scheduled window) and fires the actual alert/notification action once that condition is met. A KQL database is specifically the right fit for the stop-detection logic, rather than doing it in the Eventstream's transformation step, because detecting 'has this truck been stationary for the last 15 minutes' requires looking across a window of time-series events to compute a duration, which is exactly the time-series/windowing functionality KQL is built for -- a simple Eventstream transformation node operates on individual events as they pass through, not an accumulated time window of related prior events.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd chain this in three stages. First, the Eventstream ingests the raw GPS feed and can do light, per-event transformation on the way in. Second, that feeds an Eventhouse/KQL database, which is where the actual stop-detection logic belongs -- detecting 'this truck hasn't moved in 15 minutes' genuinely requires looking across a window of prior points for that truck, computing a duration, which is exactly the kind of time-series query KQL is designed for; an Eventstream transformation node, by contrast, only ever sees one event at a time as it passes through, with no memory of what came before it. Third, the KQL query's output feeds Activator, which is the piece that actually watches for the condition -- stop duration over 15 minutes, outside the scheduled window -- and fires the real alert. I'd also flag that 'outside a scheduled delivery window' needs the KQL logic to join against or compare to a separate schedule dataset, not just the raw GPS stream alone.
commonMistakes: Trying to detect a 15-minute stop condition in the Eventstream's transformation step alone, which lacks the time-windowed aggregation KQL provides
Forgetting Activator is the component that actually watches a condition and fires an action, not the KQL database itself
Not considering that 'outside a scheduled delivery window' needs to be joined/compared against a separate schedule dataset
Treating this as a single component instead of a chained pipeline of ingestion, time-series analysis, and alerting responsibilities
keyPoints: Eventstream handles ingestion (and light transformation) of the raw GPS feed
A KQL database/Eventhouse is where time-windowed stop-detection logic belongs, using time-series query functions
Activator is the component that watches a condition and fires the actual alert
Detecting a sustained condition over time needs time-series windowing, which a single-event transformation step can't do

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Proposes the correct chain of Fabric components in the right order
Correctly explains why KQL fits the stop-detection logic specifically
Correctly identifies Activator's role in firing the alert
Addresses the 'outside scheduled window' nuance

questions.title: Designing Topics and Partitions for a Multi-Tenant Order Platform
questions.prompt: You're designing the Kafka topic structure for an order-processing platform serving 200 retail tenants, where order events must be processed in the order they occurred within each individual tenant, but different tenants' events have no ordering relationship with each other. Propose a topic and partitioning design, and explain the one choice that actually guarantees the required per-tenant ordering.
questions.modelAnswer: One topic, orders, with a reasonable number of partitions (sized for expected throughput and consumer parallelism, not per-tenant), is generally preferable to one topic per tenant for 200 tenants, since hundreds of topics adds real operational and metadata overhead for little benefit when the only real requirement is ordering, not full isolation. The one choice that actually guarantees per-tenant ordering is the message key: producing every event with tenant_id as the Kafka message key ensures Kafka's default partitioner hashes that key deterministically to the same partition every time, and because Kafka only guarantees ordering within a single partition, never across partitions, every event for a given tenant lands on the same partition in the order it was produced, giving the required per-tenant ordering for free, while events from different tenants naturally land on different (or the same, with no ordering relationship) partitions, exactly as required. The partition count becomes a tradeoff between parallelism and per-partition ordering granularity, but doesn't affect correctness as long as the key is tenant_id.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd go with a single topic rather than 200 per-tenant topics, because the actual requirement here is ordering, not isolation, and 200 topics is real operational overhead for no benefit the requirement actually needs. The piece that matters most, though, is the message key -- every event has to be produced with tenant_id as its Kafka key, because that's what guarantees Kafka's partitioner routes all of one tenant's events to the same partition every time, deterministically. Kafka only promises ordering within a single partition, never across partitions, so by keying on tenant_id I get exactly the ordering guarantee the requirement asks for, for free, without having to build anything extra. Partition count is still a real decision, but it's a throughput/parallelism tradeoff, not a correctness one -- more partitions means more consumer parallelism, but as long as every event is keyed by tenant_id, ordering per tenant holds regardless of how many partitions the topic has.
commonMistakes: Creating one topic per tenant, which solves ordering trivially but creates unnecessary operational overhead for 200 tenants with no isolation requirement stated
Using a random or round-robin partitioner instead of keying by tenant_id, which would scatter one tenant's events across partitions and break ordering
Assuming more partitions always means better per-tenant ordering, when ordering is actually governed by the key, not partition count
Forgetting that two tenants happening to hash to the same partition is fine and expected, not a bug, since ordering is only required within a tenant
keyPoints: A single topic keyed by tenant_id is usually preferable to per-tenant topics for 200 tenants
Kafka only guarantees ordering within a single partition, never across partitions
Keying every event by tenant_id ensures all of one tenant's events land on the same partition, in order
Partition count affects throughput/parallelism, not correctness of the ordering guarantee

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Proposes a sensible topic structure (one topic, not 200)
Correctly identifies the message key as the mechanism guaranteeing ordering
Correctly explains Kafka's per-partition (not cross-partition) ordering guarantee
Correctly frames partition count as a throughput tradeoff, not an ordering one

questions.title: Moving a Team Off Local Terraform State
questions.prompt: A data platform team of six engineers has been running terraform apply from individual laptops with local state files, and it's already caused two incidents where someone applied against a stale state. Propose the fix, and explain specifically what remote state with locking adds that local state doesn't have.
questions.modelAnswer: The fix is moving to a remote backend (for an Azure-based platform, typically an Azure Storage Account container configured as the backend) with state locking enabled, rather than each engineer holding their own local terraform.tfstate file. Local state has two compounding problems: first, there's no single source of truth -- six engineers' local state files can each represent a different, possibly stale, idea of what infrastructure actually exists, so an apply from one laptop can act on an outdated picture and either fail to detect real drift or, worse, try to recreate/modify something another teammate already changed; second, there's no locking at all -- nothing prevents two people from running apply concurrently against their own (different) local copies, each racing to mutate real infrastructure with no coordination whatsoever. A remote backend fixes the first problem by giving everyone the same, current state file, read from and written to one shared location on every plan/apply. The locking a remote backend adds on top fixes the second: it acquires an exclusive lock for the duration of a plan/apply, so a second engineer's concurrent attempt is blocked (or informed) until the first one finishes, rather than both operations racing against the same shared state simultaneously -- which is actually a sharper danger with shared remote state than with disconnected local files, so locking isn't optional once state is centralized.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd move the team to a remote backend with locking, and I'd explain the fix as solving two separate problems the incidents already revealed. Local state means there's no single source of truth -- six people, six potentially different ideas of what actually exists, and an apply from any one laptop can act on a stale picture without anyone knowing until something breaks. A remote backend fixes that by centralizing to one shared, always-current state file everyone's plan and apply reads from and writes to. But centralizing alone isn't enough -- once everyone's pointed at the same shared state, now I need locking, or two people running apply at the same moment race against that one file instead of just having their own separate stale copies, which is actually a worse failure mode than what they have now. The lock that comes with most remote backends acquires exclusively for the duration of an apply, so a second attempt waits its turn instead of colliding. I'd also plan the migration carefully -- each engineer's existing local state needs to be migrated into the new backend cleanly, not just abandoned, so nothing gets lost in the transition.
commonMistakes: Moving to remote state without also enabling locking, which trades 'divergent local state' for 'concurrent corruption of one shared state'
Not migrating each engineer's existing local state into the new backend cleanly (terraform init -migrate-state), risking state loss
Assuming remote state alone prevents bad applies, when it only provides a shared source of truth and locking, not approval/review
Forgetting to restrict direct backend access so engineers can't still bypass the shared state by reverting to local
keyPoints: Local state means no single source of truth across a team, risking stale-state applies
Local state also has no locking, allowing concurrent applies to race against different copies
Remote state centralizes to one shared, current state file everyone reads/writes
Locking (part of most remote backends) prevents concurrent applies from racing against the shared state

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Proposes remote backend with locking as the fix
Correctly explains the stale/divergent local state problem
Correctly explains what locking specifically adds (preventing concurrent corruption)
Notes the migration/rollout consideration

questions.title: Structuring a Terraform Repo as the Platform Grows Past One main.tf
questions.prompt: A data platform's Terraform code started as a single main.tf and has grown to provision a storage account, a Fabric capacity, and an Event Hub, and now a second nearly-identical environment is needed for staging. Propose a module-based restructuring, and explain what specifically becomes easier once the resources are wrapped in a reusable module.
questions.modelAnswer: Restructure into a modules/ directory containing one module per logical resource group -- for example, modules/data-platform/ containing the storage account, Fabric capacity, and Event Hub definitions together, parameterized by variables like environment, location, and sku -- with separate top-level configurations per environment (environments/prod/main.tf, environments/staging/main.tf) that each simply call module "data_platform" { source = "../../modules/data-platform", environment = "staging", ... } with environment-specific variable values. What specifically becomes easier: standing up staging is no longer copy-pasting and manually editing a second full set of resource blocks (which risks the two environments silently drifting apart in configuration, with one getting a fix or change the other never receives) -- it's calling the same module twice with different inputs, guaranteeing both environments share identical resource logic and only genuinely differ in the values that should differ (names, sizes, environment tags). A bug fix or new resource added to the module automatically applies to every environment that calls it the next time each environment's own state is applied, rather than needing to be manually re-applied to each environment's separate copy of the code.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd pull the storage account, Fabric capacity, and Event Hub out of main.tf and into a shared module -- modules/data-platform -- parameterized by the things that genuinely differ between environments, like environment name, location, and SKU. Then each environment gets its own small configuration file that just calls that module with its own variable values. The real benefit shows up the moment staging needs to exist: instead of copy-pasting the old main.tf and hoping I edit every value correctly, I'm calling the identical module twice, which means staging and production are guaranteed to share the same resource logic and only differ in the inputs I explicitly varied. And when I find a bug in how the Event Hub is configured three months from now, I fix it once in the module, and every environment picks it up the next time its own state gets applied -- I'm not hunting down and patching N copies of nearly-identical code. The one thing I'd be careful not to forget is that each environment still needs its own Terraform state, even though they share the same module source.
commonMistakes: Copy-pasting the existing main.tf into a second file for staging instead of extracting a reusable module
Hardcoding environment-specific values inside the module instead of exposing them as input variables
Forgetting each environment needs its own state (and likely its own backend configuration), even though they share the same module source
Not parameterizing something that actually differs between environments (like SKU/size), defeating part of the reuse benefit
keyPoints: A shared module encapsulates the common resource logic, parameterized by variables
Separate environment-level configurations call the same module with different variable values
This prevents configuration drift between environments that manual copy-paste risks
A module fix/change applies to every calling environment on its next apply, rather than needing manual duplication

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Proposes a sensible module + per-environment-config structure
Correctly explains the configuration-drift risk this solves
Correctly explains how a module change propagates to callers
Notes that each environment still needs its own state

questions.title: Lambda or Kappa: Choosing an Architecture for a New Analytics Platform
questions.prompt: A new analytics platform needs both near-real-time dashboards (seconds of latency) and the ability to reprocess months of historical data when business logic changes. A colleague suggests the Lambda architecture; you're considering Kappa instead. Explain the real tradeoff between the two for this specific requirement.
questions.modelAnswer: Lambda architecture runs two separate pipelines side by side -- a fast/streaming path for low-latency results and a slow/batch path over the same raw data for accuracy and historical reprocessing -- with a serving layer that reconciles both. The real cost of Lambda is maintaining genuinely two implementations of the business logic (one in the streaming framework, one in the batch framework), which commonly drift apart over time as one gets updated and the other doesn't, producing subtly different numbers between 'live' and 'historical' views of the same metric -- a real, recurring maintenance burden, not a one-time cost. Kappa architecture instead treats everything as a stream: all data, including historical reprocessing, flows through the same single streaming pipeline, with reprocessing accomplished by replaying historical events from a durable, long-retention log (like Kafka with extended retention) through that same pipeline rather than maintaining a separate batch codepath. The tradeoff: Kappa requires the chosen streaming engine to genuinely handle the reprocessing workload efficiently at scale, and it requires committing to one unified processing model for every kind of workload, including ones that might be more naturally expressed as batch. For a platform explicitly needing both near-real-time dashboards and genuine historical reprocessing when logic changes, Kappa is the stronger fit specifically because it avoids the dual-implementation drift risk that's a recurring, not one-time, cost under Lambda -- but it's a real commitment to the streaming engine's reprocessing capability, which should be validated, not assumed.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd push back gently on defaulting to Lambda here, not because it's wrong in general, but because this specific requirement exposes its real weakness. Lambda means maintaining two separate implementations of the same business logic -- one written for the streaming framework, one for the batch framework -- and in my experience those two drift apart over time in ways nobody notices until a 'live' number and a 'historical' number for the same metric don't match. Kappa avoids that entirely by treating everything, including reprocessing, as a replay through the same single streaming pipeline -- there's only ever one implementation of the logic. The real cost I'd be upfront about is that Kappa leans hard on the streaming engine actually being able to replay months of history efficiently, which isn't free, and it means committing to one processing model for everything rather than letting batch-shaped work just be batch. Given this platform explicitly needs both real-time dashboards and genuine historical reprocessing, I'd lean Kappa, specifically because the dual-implementation drift Lambda creates is exactly the kind of bug this requirement would surface repeatedly.
commonMistakes: Picking Lambda by default without weighing the real, ongoing cost of maintaining two parallel implementations of the same logic
Assuming Kappa is simpler because it's 'just one pipeline,' without validating the streaming engine can actually handle large-scale historical replay
Not identifying logic drift between batch and streaming paths as Lambda's real, recurring risk, not just an upfront cost
Treating this as a binary with no acknowledgment of the real commitment Kappa makes to one processing model
keyPoints: Lambda maintains two separate pipelines (streaming + batch), risking logic drift between them over time
Kappa treats everything as a stream, with reprocessing done via replay through a durable log
Kappa avoids dual-implementation drift but requires the streaming engine to genuinely handle large-scale replay
The stated requirement (both real-time and reprocessing) specifically exposes Lambda's drift risk

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains Lambda's dual-pipeline structure and its drift risk
Correctly explains Kappa's single-stream-plus-replay model
Correctly identifies Kappa's real cost/commitment
Makes a reasoned recommendation tied to the stated requirement

questions.title: Designing an Ingestion Layer for Mixed Batch and Streaming Sources
questions.prompt: A new platform needs to ingest three kinds of sources: a nightly vendor file drop (CSV), a transactional database needing change capture, and a live clickstream. Propose an ingestion layer design that handles all three without forcing them into one identical pattern, and explain why forcing a single ingestion pattern across all three would be the wrong call.
questions.modelAnswer: Each source genuinely has a different natural shape, and the ingestion layer should respect that rather than force a single pattern: the nightly vendor CSV is a straightforward scheduled batch ingestion -- a pipeline that lands the file, validates its structure, and writes it to bronze on a schedule matching the vendor's drop cadence; the transactional database needs change data capture (CDC) rather than repeatedly querying the full table, since CDC captures just the inserts/updates/deletes since the last capture, avoiding the cost and staleness of re-pulling the whole table on every run; the live clickstream needs a genuine streaming ingestion path (an Eventstream/Kafka-style continuous consumer) because its entire value is low latency, and batching it would defeat the purpose. All three can still land in a common bronze layer structure (consistent partitioning conventions, consistent metadata columns) even though the mechanism getting them there differs -- the commonality belongs at the storage/layer-contract level, not the ingestion mechanism level. Forcing a single pattern across all three would be the wrong call because each mismatch has a real cost: forcing the clickstream into nightly batch destroys its latency value entirely; forcing the CDC source into full-table batch pulls wastes compute re-reading unchanged rows and can't give sub-day freshness even if the business later wants it; forcing the vendor file into a streaming pattern adds complexity with zero benefit, since the file only exists once a day regardless of how fast you could theoretically process it.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd design each source's ingestion to fit what it actually is, rather than forcing all three through one mechanism for the sake of consistency. The vendor CSV is simple: a scheduled batch job that lands the file and validates it against the vendor's actual drop cadence. The transactional database I'd put on change data capture rather than full-table pulls, because CDC only grabs what actually changed since last time, which is both cheaper and gives finer-grained freshness than re-reading the whole table ever could. The clickstream gets a real streaming path, because the entire reason anyone wants a clickstream is low latency, and batching it would just throw that value away. Where I would standardize is one level up, at the bronze layer itself -- consistent partitioning conventions, consistent metadata columns -- so even though three different mechanisms got the data there, what lands in bronze looks and behaves consistently. Forcing one ingestion pattern across all three would cost something real in each direction: batch the clickstream and you've killed its latency value, full-pull the transactional source and you're wasting compute re-reading unchanged rows, stream the vendor file and you've added real complexity for a source that only exists once a day no matter how fast you process it.
commonMistakes: Insisting on one ingestion tool/pattern for consistency's sake, ignoring that each source has a fundamentally different natural cadence
Using full-table pulls for the transactional database instead of CDC, wasting compute and missing finer-grained history
Batching the clickstream, destroying the entire reason it needed low latency in the first place
Not recognizing that commonality can still exist at the bronze storage layer even when ingestion mechanisms differ
keyPoints: The vendor CSV fits straightforward scheduled batch ingestion
The transactional database should use CDC, not repeated full-table pulls
The clickstream needs genuine streaming ingestion to preserve its latency value
A common bronze storage contract can unify all three even though their ingestion mechanisms differ

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Proposes the correct ingestion mechanism for each of the three sources
Correctly explains why forcing one pattern would hurt each source specifically
Notes a sensible point of commonality (bronze layer contract) despite differing mechanisms

questions.title: Databricks Structured Streaming or Fabric Real-Time Intelligence?
questions.prompt: An organization already has an established Databricks lakehouse using Structured Streaming for several pipelines, and is now evaluating whether a new real-time use case (live operational dashboards with sub-second, ad hoc KQL-style queries) should also go through Databricks Structured Streaming, or through Fabric's Eventstream/Eventhouse real-time stack instead. What would actually drive that decision?
questions.modelAnswer: Both can genuinely handle streaming ingestion and transformation, so the deciding factor isn't 'which one can stream' -- it's what the specific use case needs on the query/serving side. Structured Streaming on Databricks is excellent at continuous transformation and writing results into Delta tables, but querying those Delta tables for truly ad hoc, sub-second, exploratory queries isn't really Delta/Spark SQL's strength; Spark is optimized for large-batch and streaming transformation throughput, not low-latency ad hoc point queries. Fabric's Eventhouse/KQL database, by contrast, is specifically built for that access pattern -- a time-series-optimized store designed for exactly this kind of fast, flexible, ad hoc querying over recent streaming data, a different optimization target than Delta/Spark. The practical driver: if the new use case's defining requirement is the query pattern (sub-second ad hoc exploration), that pulls toward Fabric's real-time stack even in an org otherwise standardized on Databricks; if the defining requirement is instead heavy, complex transformation logic that then feeds existing Delta-based gold tables and reporting, staying within Structured Streaming keeps the solution inside the already-established platform and skill set. Many real implementations end up doing both, so this isn't necessarily an either-or choice at the org level, even though it is a real choice for this one specific use case.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't frame this as 'which platform can stream,' because both genuinely can -- the real question is what kind of querying this specific use case needs afterward. Structured Streaming is excellent at transformation throughput, writing continuously into Delta tables, but Delta and Spark SQL aren't really built for sub-second, ad hoc, exploratory querying -- that's not what they're optimized for. A KQL database in Fabric's Eventhouse is purpose-built for exactly that access pattern, fast and flexible querying over recent time-series data. So if this particular use case's defining need is genuinely sub-second ad hoc exploration, I'd lean toward Fabric's real-time stack for it specifically, even though the org is otherwise standardized on Databricks -- standardization is a good default, not a rule that should override what a specific workload actually needs. And I'd point out these aren't mutually exclusive at the org level: it's common to keep heavy transformation in Structured Streaming and surface a low-latency querying layer through a KQL database fed from the same underlying stream, rather than treating this as a company-wide either-or.
commonMistakes: Treating this as 'which tool can stream data' when both genuinely can -- the real question is the query/serving pattern needed
Assuming organizational standardization on Databricks should automatically decide every new streaming use case
Not recognizing that Spark/Delta and a KQL time-series store are optimized for different access patterns (transformation throughput vs. ad hoc low-latency query)
Treating the choice as mutually exclusive at the org level rather than per-use-case
keyPoints: Both platforms can genuinely handle streaming transformation; the real differentiator is the query/serving pattern
Spark/Delta is optimized for transformation throughput, not low-latency ad hoc point queries
A KQL database is purpose-built for fast, ad hoc querying over recent streaming data
The decision should be driven by this specific use case's defining requirement, not blanket platform standardization

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the query/serving pattern as the real deciding factor
Correctly characterizes what each platform is actually optimized for
Makes a reasoned, use-case-specific recommendation
Notes the two aren't necessarily mutually exclusive at the org level

questions.title: A stakeholder wants a new field added mid-sprint
questions.prompt: Your team is three days into a two-week sprint when a stakeholder asks you to add a new field to a report you're already building, saying it's 'quick, shouldn't change anything.' Walk me through how you'd actually handle this request.
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer doesn't just say yes or no -- it describes a specific process for evaluating a mid-sprint request honestly before committing to it. First, actually assess the request rather than taking 'quick' at face value: does the new field require touching the dataset's underlying query, does it interact with existing filters or parameters, does it need its own testing? Second, be transparent with the stakeholder and the team about the real tradeoff: if it genuinely is small, say so and fold it in; if it's not, explain specifically why (not vaguely) and present the actual options -- add it now and risk the sprint's committed work, or add it to the next sprint, or (if it's urgent) swap it in for something already committed and explicitly deprioritized. The point to get across is that this isn't about being rigid or unhelpful -- it's about making the tradeoff visible instead of silently absorbing scope and then explaining later why other committed work slipped.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't just say yes because it's described as quick, and I also wouldn't flatly refuse because 'that's not what we committed to' -- I'd actually go look at what the change requires first. If it really is a one-column addition to an existing dataset with no filter interactions, I'd just do it and move on, because treating every tiny request as a formal change-control event is its own kind of overhead. But if it touches the dataset's query, interacts with parameters already in play, or needs real testing, I'd say that specifically and honestly, rather than agreeing and then quietly having something else slip. I'd lay out the actual choice for the stakeholder and my Product Owner: we can add this now and something else committed to this sprint moves to next sprint, or this goes into the next sprint's backlog, or if it's genuinely urgent, I'll tell you specifically what I'd need to drop to make room for it. What I'm protecting isn't my own workload -- it's the team's ability to make an honest commitment and actually hit it, instead of everyone quietly absorbing 'just one more small thing' until the sprint's real scope bears no resemblance to what was planned.
commonMistakes: Automatically agreeing to the request without actually assessing its real scope first
Refusing rigidly without explaining the real tradeoff or offering alternatives
Silently absorbing the extra work and letting already-committed work slip without telling anyone why
Not involving the Product Owner or team in the actual tradeoff decision
keyPoints: Actually assesses the request's real scope instead of taking 'quick' at face value
Is transparent about the tradeoff rather than silently absorbing scope creep
Presents concrete options (do it now and drop something, defer it, or swap priorities)
Frames the goal as protecting the team's ability to make honest commitments, not personal workload

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes actually assessing the request's real scope rather than assuming
Shows transparent communication about the tradeoff involved
Presents concrete, realistic options rather than a flat yes/no
Frames this as protecting the team's commitments, not personal convenience

questions.title: Communicating a blocker in the daily standup
questions.prompt: You're stuck on a task -- a stored procedure change you need is waiting on another team's approval -- and it's been blocked for two days. How would you bring this up in the daily standup, and what would you do about it outside of standup?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer treats the Daily Scrum correctly -- as a short team sync, not a status report to a manager -- and keeps the standup update itself brief and specific: what's blocked, who or what it's waiting on, and how long it's been stuck, rather than a long explanation of the underlying technical problem. The real work happens outside standup: actually escalating the blocker rather than just mentioning it and waiting -- following up directly with whoever owns the approval, looping in the Scrum Master if the blocker is specifically the kind of cross-team obstacle they're meant to help clear, and being honest with the team about the sprint-goal impact if it stays stuck much longer, rather than quietly hoping it resolves itself. The key distinction a strong answer draws is between mentioning a blocker (passive) and actively working to clear it (what's actually expected).
questions.professionalAnswer: In standup itself, I'd keep it tight: 'I'm blocked on the stored procedure change -- it's been waiting on sign-off from the other team for two days now, and I don't have a resolution plan yet.' That's it -- standup isn't the place to walk through the technical details or vent about how annoying the wait is; it's a quick sync so the team knows where things stand. The actual work happens right after standup, not during it. I'd go directly to whoever on the other team owns that approval and ask specifically what's holding it up and when I can expect it, rather than just waiting passively for two more days. If that doesn't move things, I'd loop in my Scrum Master specifically, because clearing exactly this kind of cross-team blocker is their job, not something I should be expected to just push through alone. And if it looks like this is going to threaten the sprint goal, I'd say that out loud to the team well before the sprint review, not as a surprise at the end -- being blocked isn't a failure on my part, but sitting on it quietly without escalating would be.
commonMistakes: Treating the standup as the place to explain the full technical backstory instead of a brief status
Mentioning the blocker in standup but then passively waiting instead of actively escalating it afterward
Not involving the Scrum Master, whose job specifically includes clearing cross-team blockers
Waiting until the sprint review to surface that the blocker threatened the sprint goal
keyPoints: The Daily Scrum update should be brief and specific, not a technical deep dive
Mentioning a blocker in standup isn't the same as actively working to clear it
Escalating directly to the other team and/or the Scrum Master is the appropriate next step
Sprint-goal risk should be surfaced early, not held until the sprint review

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes an appropriately brief, specific standup update
Describes actively escalating the blocker outside of standup, not just waiting
Correctly involves the Scrum Master's actual role in clearing blockers
Shows early, honest communication about sprint-goal risk

questions.title: Two stakeholders both want their ticket done first
questions.prompt: You have two open tickets: a bug fix a sales manager is pushing for urgently, and a new report feature your own manager assigned last week with a deadline that's actually sooner. Both stakeholders think their request is the priority. How do you handle it?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer doesn't unilaterally decide between two stakeholders' competing priorities on its own authority -- it recognizes that prioritization decisions belong with whoever actually owns the backlog's priority order (a Product Owner, in Scrum terms, or whoever plays that role on the team), and surfaces the conflict to them explicitly rather than quietly picking one and hoping the other doesn't notice. The practical first step is gathering the actual facts needed to make the decision -- how urgent is the bug really (is it actively breaking something for users right now, or just annoying), and what's the real deadline and consequence of missing it for the report feature -- rather than just taking either stakeholder's framing of urgency at face value. Then bring both pieces of information to whoever should decide, make the conflict and the tradeoff explicit, and get an actual decision rather than silently deprioritizing one person's request without them knowing.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't try to quietly referee this myself between two people who each think their thing is most important -- that's not actually my call to make alone, and if I just pick one, I've effectively made a business priority decision without the authority or the full context to make it well. My first step is getting the real facts: is this bug actually breaking something in production right now, or is it an annoyance that feels urgent but isn't actually blocking anyone? What's the real, hard deadline on the report feature, and what actually happens if it slips a few days? Once I have real answers instead of just each stakeholder's own sense of urgency, I'd go to whoever actually owns prioritization for my work -- my manager, or a Product Owner if that's how the team is structured -- lay out both asks and their actual urgency side by side, and ask for an explicit call. I'd rather spend ten minutes getting a clear decision than spend a day guessing which stakeholder to disappoint and then having to explain that choice after the fact.
commonMistakes: Unilaterally deciding between two stakeholders' competing priorities without the authority or full context to do so
Taking either stakeholder's self-reported urgency at face value instead of verifying the actual impact and deadline
Quietly deprioritizing one request without telling that stakeholder, letting them find out later
Not escalating to whoever actually owns prioritization decisions for the team's work
keyPoints: Prioritization conflicts between stakeholders should be escalated, not unilaterally resolved
Gathers real facts about urgency and deadlines rather than accepting either framing at face value
Brings both pieces of information to whoever owns the priority decision for an explicit call
Avoids silently deprioritizing a stakeholder without their knowledge

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Recognizes this isn't a unilateral decision and escalates appropriately
Describes gathering real facts about urgency/impact before escalating
Describes a clear, explicit escalation with both pieces of information presented
Avoids silently disappointing either stakeholder without communication

questions.title: A ticket has no acceptance criteria
questions.prompt: You pick up a ticket from the sprint backlog that says 'Add a filter for region to the sales dashboard' with no further detail -- no acceptance criteria, no mention of default behavior or how it should interact with existing filters. What do you do before writing any code?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer resists the temptation to just start building based on a guess, because a story without acceptance criteria is genuinely too vague to know when it's actually done -- 'I think this is done' and a shared, checkable definition of done are different things, and building against the wrong assumption wastes real time for both the developer and whoever has to send it back. The right move is going back to whoever owns the ticket -- the Product Owner or the stakeholder who requested it -- and asking specific, concrete questions rather than one vague 'what do you mean': what should the filter's default value be, does it need to interact with (cascade from or into) any existing filters already on the dashboard, and is there a specific list of regions or should it reflect whatever's in the data. Writing those answers down as explicit acceptance criteria before starting, not after, turns a vague request into something both the developer and whoever reviews the finished work can actually check against.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't start building off a guess, because 'add a filter for region' sounds simple but actually hides several real decisions -- what region data source is sensible as the dropdown's default, whether this filter needs to interact with any filter already on the dashboard, whether 'region' even means the same thing across every table the dashboard touches. Guessing wrong on any of those means I build something, it gets reviewed, and it comes back with changes -- which is slower overall than just asking upfront. So before writing anything, I'd go back to whoever owns the ticket with specific questions, not a vague 'can you clarify this' -- I'd ask directly: should this default to the viewer's own region if we track that, does selecting a region need to affect any other filter already on the page, and is there an existing region list I should match or is this open-ended. Once I have real answers, I'd write them down as the ticket's acceptance criteria myself if nobody else does, specifically so there's a shared, checkable definition everyone agrees to before I start -- that protects me too, since I now have something concrete to point back to if the request changes later.
commonMistakes: Starting to build based on a guess instead of clarifying ambiguous requirements first
Asking a vague 'can you clarify this ticket' instead of specific, concrete questions
Not writing down the clarified requirements as explicit acceptance criteria before starting
Assuming the ticket's brevity means the request is actually simple, missing the real decisions hidden inside it
keyPoints: A story without acceptance criteria is genuinely too vague to know when it's actually done
Asks specific, concrete clarifying questions rather than a vague request for more detail
Writes down the clarified requirements as explicit acceptance criteria before starting work
Clarifying upfront is faster overall than building on a guess and having it sent back

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Recognizes the ticket is too ambiguous to build from directly
Asks specific, concrete clarifying questions rather than a vague request
Describes writing down clarified requirements as explicit acceptance criteria
Explains why clarifying upfront saves time overall

questions.title: The Business Says the Dashboard You Built Isn't What They Asked For
questions.prompt: You finish a dashboard, it passes your own testing, and then the business stakeholder reviews it in UAT and says it doesn't actually answer what they needed. How do you respond, and how do you prevent the same gap next time?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer treats a UAT rejection as a normal, expected signal rather than a personal failure or a sign the stakeholder is being difficult — UAT exists specifically to catch the case where code is technically correct but isn't actually what the business needed, which is a different question than QA's "does it work correctly" entirely. The right immediate response is to ask specific, concrete questions rather than getting defensive: what exactly does the current version show, what were they expecting instead, and can they point to a specific number or view that's wrong relative to their mental model. Often the real gap traces back to acceptance criteria that were vague or incomplete at the start, not a build mistake — which is the actual thing to fix going forward: writing more specific, checkable acceptance criteria during intake (edge cases included, like what a zero-sales region should display) so UAT becomes a confirmation step rather than where requirements gaps first surface.
questions.professionalAnswer: First thing I'd do is not get defensive about it, because UAT rejecting something isn't the same as me having done something wrong — it's literally what that stage is for, catching the gap between 'this is technically correct' and 'this is actually what we needed,' which are genuinely different questions. I'd ask specific questions rather than just apologizing and reworking blindly: what exactly were you expecting to see here, can you show me a specific number that looks wrong to you versus what you expected. Usually when I dig into it, the real root cause isn't that I built the wrong thing technically — it's that the original request or acceptance criteria were vague enough that I made a reasonable assumption that just wasn't the assumption they were making. Going forward, the actual fix isn't 'be more careful next time,' it's writing tighter, more specific acceptance criteria up front — including the edge cases, like what happens when a region has zero sales for the month — so that gap gets caught during planning instead of surfacing for the first time in UAT.
commonMistakes: Treating a UAT rejection as a personal failure or getting defensive instead of investigating specifically
Reworking the dashboard based on a vague complaint without asking specific clarifying questions first
Not tracing the root cause back to incomplete acceptance criteria, repeating the same gap on the next project
Assuming the stakeholder is simply wrong instead of taking their feedback as a genuine signal about the request
keyPoints: UAT exists specifically to catch 'technically correct but not what was needed,' a different question than QA
The right response is specific clarifying questions, not defensiveness or blind rework
The root cause is often vague acceptance criteria at intake, not a build mistake
The real fix is tighter acceptance criteria going forward, including edge cases

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Responds professionally and non-defensively to the rejection
Describes asking specific clarifying questions
Correctly identifies the likely root cause (acceptance criteria gap)
Proposes a concrete prevention for next time

questions.title: Receiving Pointed Feedback on Your Own SQL in a Pull Request
questions.prompt: You open a pull request with a new T-SQL view, confident it's correct. A senior teammate leaves a pointed comment: "This JOIN will double-count revenue whenever an order has more than one line item — did you test this against real data?" How do you respond?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer treats this as useful, correct technical feedback to actually verify, not as a tone problem to get defensive about, even though the comment reads a little sharp. The right first move is to actually check the claim against real data rather than arguing or immediately agreeing out of deference — running the query against a test order known to have multiple line items and confirming whether revenue is in fact double-counted. If the reviewer is right, which a join producing row-level duplication against a different grain often is, the response is a straightforward acknowledgment and a fix, not an excuse, and ideally a brief note on what testing step would have caught this before opening the PR (so the lesson generalizes beyond this one query). If, after checking, the claim turns out to be wrong, the response is still calm and specific: showing the actual test data and result that demonstrates the join is correct, rather than taking either the criticism or one's own original confidence at face value.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first reaction wouldn't be to get defensive about the tone — it would be to actually go test what they're describing, because it's a specific, checkable technical claim, and the only thing that actually matters here is whether it's true. I'd grab (or construct) an order with two or three line items and run the query against it specifically, checking whether the revenue total for that order comes out right or genuinely doubled. If they're right, which is honestly pretty likely given how common this exact mistake is when joining a header table to a detail table without aggregating first, I'd just say so directly — 'you're right, confirmed it with a multi-line-item order, fixing it now' — and actually fix it, rather than getting into any back-and-forth about whether the comment was blunt. If I test it and it turns out the join is actually fine for some reason they didn't account for, I'd show them the specific test case and result that proves it, calmly, rather than either caving to seniority or digging in defensively without evidence either way.
commonMistakes: Getting defensive about the comment's tone instead of verifying the actual technical claim
Agreeing immediately out of deference to seniority without actually testing the claim
Dismissing the feedback without testing it, assuming the original code must be correct
Fixing the issue without understanding why it happened, risking the same mistake on a future query
keyPoints: The right first step is verifying the specific technical claim against real data
A correct criticism should be acknowledged directly and fixed, not argued with
If the claim turns out wrong, the response should be a calm, evidence-based explanation
The goal is determining what's true, not managing how the feedback felt

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Responds by verifying the claim rather than reacting to tone
Describes a concrete way to test the claim
Shows how to respond if the criticism is correct
Shows how to respond if the criticism turns out incorrect

questions.title: A Dashboard Goes Live, and Immediately Something's Wrong
questions.prompt: Two days after a new regional revenue dashboard launches, a regional manager reports it's showing zero sales for their region, which is obviously wrong. Walk through how you'd investigate this and what you'd communicate to the regional manager while you're still figuring it out.
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer separates the investigation from the communication, and gets both moving in parallel rather than going silent until the fix is found. On investigation, the logical order is checking the environments closest to the symptom first: is this specific region's data actually present in the underlying source as of the relevant date, did the scheduled refresh for this model actually complete successfully (checking refresh history for errors), and does any report-level filter (RLS, a regional filter default) unintentionally exclude this region's rows. On communication, the mistake to avoid is going quiet until the root cause is fully found — the right move is an immediate, honest acknowledgment that specifically names what's being checked ("I've confirmed the issue and I'm checking whether it's a refresh failure or a filter problem, I'll update you within the hour") rather than either a vague "looking into it" or disappearing until there's a complete answer, since a specific update lets the regional manager decide what to do in the meantime (for example, whether to trust other numbers from the same report).
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd do two things essentially at the same time: start investigating, and send the regional manager something specific right away rather than going quiet until I have a full answer. On the investigation side, I'd work from the symptom outward — first checking refresh history to see whether last night's scheduled refresh for this model actually succeeded, since a failed or partial refresh is a really common cause of 'this one region looks wrong.' If the refresh is fine, I'd check whether the region's data is actually present in the source table for the relevant date, and then check whether any filter — RLS, a default slicer, anything report-level — is quietly excluding that region specifically. On the communication side, I'd send something concrete almost immediately, like 'I've confirmed something's wrong with the regional number, I'm checking whether it's a refresh issue or a filter issue right now, I'll have an update for you within the hour' — specific enough that they know I've actually looked at it and know roughly when to expect more, rather than a vague 'we're on it' that tells them nothing.
commonMistakes: Going silent until the root cause is fully found instead of sending a specific interim update
Guessing at the cause instead of checking refresh history and filters methodically
Sending a vague 'we're looking into it' instead of naming what's specifically being checked
Fixing the symptom without identifying why it happened, risking a repeat next refresh cycle
keyPoints: Investigation and communication should happen in parallel, not sequentially
A methodical check order: refresh history, source data presence, then report-level filters
A specific interim update is far more useful than a vague one or silence
The regional manager should know roughly when to expect a further update

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes a methodical, logically ordered investigation
Describes a specific, honest interim communication, not silence or vagueness
Recognizes investigation and communication should happen together
Mentions follow-up to prevent recurrence

questions.title: Explaining a Failed Pipeline to a Non-Technical Stakeholder
questions.prompt: A nightly pipeline that feeds the VP of Sales' Monday morning revenue report failed over the weekend, and the data is now a day stale. The VP doesn't know what 'the DAG failed' means and just wants to know if the number they're about to present to the board is right. How do you explain this to them?
questions.modelAnswer: The right approach leads with the business-relevant answer, not the technical cause: is the number right or not, and if not, by how much and since when. Translate the failure into plain language -- 'the report currently reflects data through Saturday, not Sunday, because a scheduled data load didn't complete overnight; we caught it this morning and are fixing it now' -- rather than any mention of DAGs, tasks, or retries, which mean nothing to the VP and don't answer their actual question. Give a concrete timeline for when corrected data will be available, and if the board meeting is before that, be explicit about the practical choice (present with a clear caveat about the date, or delay by a specific number of hours) rather than letting the VP walk in not knowing the number is stale. Avoid minimizing it as 'just a glitch' if it genuinely affects the number they're about to use, and follow up afterward with a brief, non-technical note on what caused it and what's being done to prevent a repeat.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd lead with exactly what they actually asked -- is the number right -- before explaining anything about why it isn't. Something like: 'The report you're about to present is showing data through Saturday, not Sunday, because an overnight data load didn't finish -- we found it this morning and expect it fixed by 10am.' No DAGs, no task names, nothing that requires them to know anything about how the pipeline works, because that's not what they asked and it wouldn't help them make their decision. If the board meeting is before that fix lands, I'd say so plainly and give them the actual choice: present with a one-line caveat about the date, or push the meeting slightly if that's an option -- I wouldn't make that call for them, but I also wouldn't leave them walking in not knowing. Afterward, I'd send a short, plain-language note on what caused it and what I'm doing so it doesn't happen again, without turning it into a technical postmortem they didn't ask for.
commonMistakes: Explaining the technical cause (DAG, task, retry) before answering the business question (is the number right)
Minimizing a real staleness issue instead of being direct about exactly what it affects
Not giving a concrete ETA for when corrected data will be available
Leaving the VP to walk into the board meeting without knowing the number might be stale
keyPoints: Lead with the business-relevant answer (is the number right, by how much is it off) before any technical explanation
Translate the failure into plain, non-technical language
Give a concrete timeline for resolution, and flag it clearly if the deadline is before that
Follow up with a brief, non-technical prevention note afterward

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Leads with the business-relevant answer rather than technical detail
Explains the failure in genuinely non-technical language
Gives a concrete timeline and addresses the deadline conflict directly
Mentions appropriate follow-up afterward

questions.title: Pushing Back on a Rushed Production Schema Change
questions.prompt: Your manager asks you to add a new required (non-nullable) column to a production Delta table that three other teams' pipelines read from, and wants it live by end of day for a dashboard demo tomorrow. You're fairly sure this will break at least one of those pipelines. How do you handle this?
questions.modelAnswer: The right approach is neither silent compliance nor a flat refusal -- it's actually verifying the concern first, raising it clearly, and offering a workable alternative. First, quickly check whether any of the three downstream pipelines explicitly SELECT * or otherwise assume today's exact schema shape, which is specifically what a new non-nullable column risks breaking, rather than asserting a risk without evidence. Then raise the specific, concrete risk to the manager directly and promptly: name which pipeline(s) are actually likely to break and why, rather than a vague 'this could break things.' Offer a real alternative that gets the actual goal -- the demo -- without the production risk: add the column as nullable (satisfying the new need without breaking anything expecting the old shape), or add it to a new/separate table the demo can read from, deploying the full non-nullable version on a normal schedule with the other teams notified first. The point is surfacing the tradeoff with a workable alternative, not just saying no, giving the manager an actual decision to make with the real risk visible.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't just do it because it's the request, and I wouldn't just refuse either -- I'd go check what I actually suspect first. I'd quickly look at whether any of the three downstream pipelines do something like SELECT * that assumes today's exact schema, since that's specifically the pattern a new non-nullable column breaks. If I confirm that risk, I'd go back to my manager with something specific, not vague -- 'this will likely break Team B's nightly load because it does a SELECT * into a typed destination, here's why' -- rather than just saying 'this feels risky.' Then I'd offer the alternative that still gets them their demo: add the column as nullable instead, which satisfies what the dashboard needs without breaking anything expecting the current shape, or point the demo at a separate table if even that's not fast enough. I want my manager making that call with the real tradeoff in front of them, not me either quietly complying with something I think will break, or refusing without giving them another way to get what they actually need by tomorrow.
commonMistakes: Silently complying with the rushed request despite being fairly sure it will break something
Flatly refusing without offering an alternative that still gets the demo its outcome
Raising a vague 'this is risky' concern instead of naming the specific pipelines and why they'd break
Not actually verifying which downstream pipelines are at risk before escalating, asserting a guess as fact
keyPoints: Verify the specific risk (which pipelines, why) before raising it, rather than asserting a vague concern
Raise the concrete risk to the manager directly and promptly
Offer a workable alternative (nullable column, or a separate table) that still achieves the actual goal
Frame this as surfacing a tradeoff for a decision, not simply refusing

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes verifying the specific risk before raising it
Describes raising the concern directly and concretely, not vaguely
Proposes a workable alternative that still achieves the goal
Frames this as a tradeoff decision, not a flat refusal

questions.title: Explaining Why 'Just Make It Real-Time' Isn't Free
questions.prompt: A product manager asks why the current daily-batch inventory dashboard can't just be switched to real-time streaming 'since Kafka is already being used elsewhere in the company.' How do you explain the actual tradeoff involved without simply saying no?
questions.modelAnswer: The right approach doesn't just say no, and doesn't just say yes to avoid a hard conversation -- it clarifies what business problem 'real-time' is actually meant to solve first, since that changes the answer: is a decision being made on stale data right now specifically, or is this a nice-to-have framed as a requirement. Then explain the real, concrete cost honestly: moving from daily batch to streaming isn't a flag to flip -- it means redesigning the ingestion layer to consume continuously rather than read once a day, redesigning the transformation logic to handle out-of-order and late-arriving events (something a daily batch job never has to think about), and taking on ongoing operational cost (a pipeline that runs continuously rather than once a night, with its own monitoring and on-call burden). 'Kafka is already being used elsewhere' doesn't change any of that -- it means infrastructure exists, not that this dashboard's pipeline is free to build or maintain. If the actual business need is 'fresher than once a day' rather than genuinely real-time, a middle option (hourly micro-batches, for instance) often gets most of the value at a fraction of the engineering and ongoing cost, worth proposing as a genuine alternative rather than framing it as real-time-or-nothing.
questions.professionalAnswer: Before answering at all, I'd ask what's actually driving the request -- is there a specific decision being made right now on data that's too stale, or is 'real-time' just sounding appealing because the word is in the air? That changes everything about the right answer. Assuming it's a real need, I'd be upfront that 'Kafka is already used elsewhere' doesn't make this free -- it means the infrastructure exists, not that this specific pipeline doesn't need its own real engineering work: continuous ingestion instead of a nightly read, transformation logic that now has to deal with events arriving late or out of order, which a once-a-day batch job never has to think about at all, and an ongoing operational cost of running and monitoring something continuously instead of once a night. If what they actually need is 'fresher than once a day' rather than truly real-time, I'd propose hourly batches as a real middle option -- it gets most of the practical benefit for a fraction of the build and ongoing cost, and I'd rather offer that than leave them thinking it's streaming or nothing.
commonMistakes: Saying yes just to avoid a difficult conversation about cost and effort
Saying no without explaining the actual tradeoff in terms the PM can evaluate
Assuming existing Kafka infrastructure elsewhere means this specific pipeline is free to build
Not proposing a middle-ground option (e.g. hourly batches) when genuine real-time isn't actually required
keyPoints: Clarify what business problem 'real-time' is actually meant to solve before answering
Explain the real engineering/operational cost honestly and specifically: continuous ingestion, out-of-order/late-event handling, ongoing operational burden
Existing infrastructure elsewhere doesn't make this pipeline's build/maintenance free
A middle-ground option (more frequent batches) often satisfies the real need at much lower cost

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Clarifies the actual underlying business need first
Explains the real engineering/operational cost honestly and specifically
Correctly notes existing infrastructure doesn't make this free
Proposes a reasonable middle-ground alternative

questions.title: A Teammate Keeps Making Manual Portal Changes Instead of Updating Terraform
questions.prompt: You discover that a teammate has been making quick fixes directly in the Azure portal instead of through the team's Terraform code, because 'it's faster for small things.' The next terraform plan now wants to revert several of those changes. How do you address this with them?
questions.modelAnswer: This is worth a direct, non-confrontational conversation, not a passive-aggressive revert or a complaint to a manager first. Start by understanding their actual reasoning rather than assuming carelessness -- 'it's faster for small things' usually means the Terraform workflow (plan, review, apply) feels like too much overhead for a one-line config tweak, which is a legitimate friction point worth acknowledging rather than dismissing. Explain the concrete cost of what just happened, specifically: terraform plan now wants to revert real, intentional changes because the code and reality have drifted apart, and if that plan had been applied without anyone noticing, it would have silently undone their fix -- that's the actual risk manual portal changes create, not an abstract rule. Agree on a shared path forward: for genuinely urgent fixes, there should be an agreed process (make the manual fix if truly urgent, then immediately open a PR updating the Terraform to match, same day) rather than either 'never touch the portal' (unrealistic for genuine emergencies) or 'manual changes are fine' (which is what caused the drift). The goal is a workable norm the whole team can actually follow, not a one-time scolding.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd go talk to them directly rather than just silently reverting the drift or escalating to a manager first. I'd start by actually understanding why -- 'it's faster for small things' usually means the full plan-review-apply cycle feels like overkill for a one-line tweak, and that's a real friction point, not laziness, so I wouldn't lead with a lecture. Then I'd show them the concrete thing that just happened: terraform plan is now trying to revert their actual, intentional fix, because the code doesn't know about it -- and if someone had applied that plan without noticing, it would have silently undone the work they just did. That's the real risk, not an abstract 'we have a process' rule. From there I'd want us to agree on something practical together: if a fix is genuinely urgent, make it in the portal if you have to, but open a PR to match it in Terraform the same day, so the drift never has a chance to surface later as a surprise revert. I'd rather land on a norm we both actually follow than either pretend the portal should never be touched or let this keep happening quietly.
commonMistakes: Reverting the drift silently without talking to the teammate about why it happened
Assuming carelessness instead of understanding the actual friction that led to the manual change
Treating this as 'never touch the portal, ever' with no accommodation for genuine emergencies
Not agreeing on a concrete, repeatable process going forward, just addressing this one incident
keyPoints: Understand the teammate's actual reasoning rather than assuming carelessness
Explain the concrete risk (Terraform plan silently reverting a real, intentional change) rather than an abstract rule
Propose a realistic shared process for genuinely urgent fixes (manual fix, then immediate matching PR)
Aim for a workable team norm, not a one-time correction

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Approaches this as a direct, understanding conversation rather than a silent revert or escalation
Explains the concrete risk the drift created
Proposes a realistic process for urgent fixes going forward
Frames the goal as a sustainable team norm

questions.title: Owning a Mistake That Shipped Bad Data to Production
questions.prompt: You deployed a silver-layer transformation last week that had a subtle bug -- it was silently dropping about 2% of orders that had a null discount_code, which you didn't catch before release. A stakeholder just noticed the gold-layer totals don't reconcile with the source system. How do you handle owning this?
questions.modelAnswer: The right approach is to own it directly and specifically the moment it's confirmed, rather than being defensive, minimizing it, or waiting to be asked more pointed questions. Confirm the actual scope first -- how many records, over what time range, which downstream reports are affected -- so the message to the stakeholder is concrete rather than a vague apology: 'I found a bug in last week's deployment that's been dropping about 2% of orders with a missing discount code since the 14th; it affects the gold revenue totals for that period, and here's the corrected number' is categorically more useful than 'sorry, something went wrong.' Fix the root cause (the transformation logic should flag or default a missing discount_code rather than silently filtering the row out) and reprocess the affected historical gold-layer data so the numbers are actually corrected, not just going forward. Separately, without turning it into empty self-criticism, identify what testing step would have caught this before release -- a row-count or null-rate check comparing bronze to silver, which is exactly the kind of check this incident reveals was missing -- so the same category of bug is less likely to ship silently again.
questions.professionalAnswer: The moment I confirm this, I'd own it directly -- no minimizing, no waiting for someone to ask a more pointed question before admitting the actual scope. But before I say anything to the stakeholder, I'd quickly quantify it: how many records, what date range, which reports downstream are affected, so what I tell them is concrete instead of a vague apology. Something like 'I found a bug in last week's deployment that's been dropping about 2% of orders with a missing discount code since the 14th -- here's the corrected number for the affected period' is just more useful to them than 'sorry, looking into it.' Then I'd fix the actual root cause -- the transformation should flag or default a missing discount_code instead of silently filtering the row out -- and reprocess the historical gold data that was affected, not just fix it going forward and leave the past numbers wrong. And without turning this into self-flagellation, I'd genuinely ask what testing step would have caught this before it shipped -- probably a basic row-count or null-rate check comparing bronze to silver -- because that's the concrete thing that makes this less likely to happen again, not just 'I'll be more careful.'
commonMistakes: Being defensive or minimizing the issue instead of directly owning it once confirmed
Reporting the problem vaguely instead of quantifying the actual scope and impact
Fixing the code going forward without reprocessing the already-affected historical data
Not identifying a concrete testing/monitoring gap that would catch this category of bug earlier next time
keyPoints: Own the mistake directly and specifically once confirmed, without defensiveness or minimizing
Quantify the actual scope (how many records, what time range, which reports) before communicating
Fix the root cause and reprocess affected historical data, not just the code going forward
Identify a concrete prevention step (e.g., a bronze-to-silver row/null-count check) for next time

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Owns the mistake directly and specifically
Quantifies scope and impact concretely before communicating
Describes fixing root cause and reprocessing historical data
Proposes a concrete prevention step for next time
